#6434. The U.S. just lost its measles elimination status. What now?

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The virus, eliminated in 2000, has now been circulating for more than a year

Flyers provide information about a Pennsylvania Department of Health measles vaccination clinic in Lancaster County aiming to curb an ongoing outbreak.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

The highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

That won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” said epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

“To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

While mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

The measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

That measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and quickly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”

What’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, said in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”

But surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo said. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health

Efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo says. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, says Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

Measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer said in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive plan at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo says. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”

There’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

“The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo says. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has said the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”

Eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo says. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in New Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also announced that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

“It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”

#6433. These ants grow enormous heads, but their antennae break a rule of biology

Soldier ants grow heads twice as wide as a worker's, yet their antennae span exactly the same sizes, and colony signals help set them.

A bigger animal comes with bigger parts. A big dog has a big head, big paws, and a big tail, and the same goes for nearly every creature biologists have measured.

In one of the most diverse groups of ants on Earth, the soldiers don’t follow that pattern.

Their antennae come in the same sizes as the antennae of the much smaller workers, and the colony’s own chemical signals help shape how big each antenna grows.

A graduate student spotted it by accident under a microscope. Erica Vong, a researcher in Rajendhran Rajakumar’s lab at the University of Ottawa, showed him the antennae of two ants, and the smaller antenna belonged to the soldier.

“Much like when you are getting your favorite latte, both castes have small, medium, and large sizes of overlapping antennae,” said Rajakumar, an associate professor in the university’s Department of Biology.

The ants belong to Pheidole, the big-headed ants. Each colony has two kinds of worker: small minors and much larger soldiers whose heads are about twice as wide.

Soldiers defend the nest and mill seeds, and workers do most of the rest.

Rajakumar’s team measured 100 workers and 100 soldiers of one Florida species, Pheidole dentata. For body size they used the width of the thorax just behind the head.

For the antenna they used its first segment, the long stalk that gives an ant’s antenna its elbow shape.

Soldiers had wider bodies and far wider heads, as expected. Their antenna stalks, though, were the same length on average as the workers’, and the whole antenna followed the same pattern.

The two castes’ measurements overlapped so completely that the team couldn’t tell them apart.

Within each caste the old rule still held. A bigger worker had a bigger antenna than a smaller worker, and the same was true among soldiers.

Pooled together, the numbers showed no link between antenna and body at all, and the trend only reappeared once the castes were split apart.

Queens were the exception, with larger bodies and larger antennae than either worker caste.

To see whether one species was a fluke, the team pulled published measurements for 565 Pheidole species from the Americas.

Across the 565 species, soldiers and workers often had antenna stalks of similar length, even though soldiers consistently had wider heads.

For each species, Rajakumar’s team divided the soldier’s antenna stalk by the worker’s. The most common answer was one, meaning no difference at all, with some species a little above and some a little below.

The same calculation for head width most often came out at 2 to 1, and no species came in under 1.4 to 1.

The team then measured ants from 14 other genera in three subfamilies, using live colonies, specimens from the Cornell University Insect Collection, and photographs from an online ant database.

In species with no soldier caste, and in most that evolved one on their own, antennae grew with the body as usual.

The one exception was a turtle ant, Cephalotes varians, a close relative of Pheidole. The authors suggest the decoupling first appeared in the common ancestor the two groups share.

Whether a Pheidole larva becomes a worker or a soldier depends on how well it eats. A well-fed larva ends up with more juvenile hormone, and a high enough level turns it into a soldier.

Adult soldiers give off a pheromone that pushes the other way, so a colony with plenty of soldiers makes fewer new ones.

The team tested both signals on larvae from lab colonies collected in Gainesville, Florida, and kept at 77°F (25°C) on a diet of mealworms and crickets.

They dabbed some larvae with a synthetic version of the hormone and raised each one with either two adult workers or two adult soldiers, starting with 40 larvae per condition.

The larvae were about a twentieth of an inch (1 to 1.5 millimeters) long, young enough that either fate was still open.

Hormone-treated larvae raised by workers became soldiers with a normal spread of antenna sizes.

Larvae raised by soldiers without the hormone became workers smaller than any found in a natural colony, with antennae to match. The team calls them nanoworkers.

“Social signals and hormones do more than determine whether an ant becomes a worker or a soldier,” Rajakumar said.

“They can also reshape how different traits grow and scale together (or decouple), within castes, between castes, and more broadly across species.”

Larvae that had already passed the point of no return toward becoming soldiers gave the stranger result.

Raised by soldiers, they emerged with soldier-sized heads on worker-sized bodies, and with antenna stalks shorter than those of the smallest natural workers. The team calls these nanosoldiers.

A developing soldier briefly grows a stub of a wing that never becomes a wing, and that stub acts as a signaling center that helps set the soldier’s big head.

When the team switched off a gene that drives that stub, the larvae grew into smaller ants with smaller heads. Their antennae came out at nearly one size, with almost none of the usual spread.

The team has not found a nanoworker or a nanosoldier in the wild. The authors suspect selection weeds them out.

A soldier’s head on a worker’s body may not be properly supported, and an antenna that small may carry too few sensory hairs to do its job.

The authors also allow that the hidden potential could be a side effect of selection on something else, and the question of which is open.

An ant’s antennae are its main contact with the world. They pick up trail and alarm pheromones, touch, heat, humidity, and vibration, and ants use them to tell nestmates from strangers.

The elbow stalk matters too, because an ant swings it to aim the sensitive tip at whatever it is exploring. The stalk’s length sets where that elbow sits, which affects how an ant probes and follows a trail.

A longer antenna carries more sensory hairs, and earlier work found that how an ant responds to an intruder depends on how many of those hairs it has.

So a colony whose members span a range of antenna sizes may span a range of sensitivities as well.

Rajakumar’s team offers one explanation for why the two castes share a range. When a Pheidole colony runs short of workers, its soldiers take on worker jobs, including caring for young.

Soldiers with the same spread of antenna sizes as workers may make that switch more easily. Once the next generation restores the balance, they can go back to defense.

“The antenna is not simply getting bigger because the ant is bigger,” Rajakumar said.

“In these colonies, development preserves a flexible range of antennal forms that may help individuals compatibly respond together to changing environmental demands.”

The authors wrote that the adaptive role of the decoupling is still unclear, and the job-switching idea is a hypothesis they haven’t tested.

Their hormone and pheromone experiments used one species, Pheidole dentata.

Roughly half the treated larvae died before reaching adulthood, which the authors attribute to raising each larva with only two adults instead of a full colony.

Antenna length was measured, not the sensory hairs on it, so whether a soldier’s small antenna senses what a worker’s does is still an open question.

The evolutionary story also rests on a single turtle ant species. And 59 Pheidole species were left out of the genus-wide count because one caste or the other had no published measurement.

Checking the relatives is the next step the authors name.

If antennae turn out to be decoupled across the turtle ants and a third genus, Procryptocerus, the pattern would date back to the ancestor of all three.

Until someone measures those ants, the origin stays a hypothesis.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft just reached 1 light-day from our planet, but a newfound glitch in the probe's onboard computer is preventing it from sharing science data with Earth.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has confirmed that its Voyager 1 spacecraft has reached a record-breaking 1 light-day from Earth — but new milestones come with old problems.

On Nov. 14, the Voyager mission team discovered that the nearly 50-year-old space probe had stopped sending science data back to Earth, according to NASA — a problem that the team had to deal with as recently as 2024. As of Thursday (Nov. 19), the team had not resolved the problem.

But they did detect a "carrier" signal that is used to ferry science and engineering information from Voyager 1 to Earth, confirming that the probe is still powered up and pointed in the right direction.

"We have an anomaly that is not unseen before," Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager, said at a NASA news conference Thursday, adding that she is "confident" that the science data will continue flowing again soon.

Using the carrier signal, the team confirmed that the probe had reached its latest distance milestone of 1 light-day from Earth, or roughly 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) away, Wednesday (Nov. 18). At this distance, which no human-made object had ever reached before, it takes a full 24 hours for radio signals traveling at the speed of light to get from Earth to Voyager 1 and vice versa. (The spacecraft's twin probe, Voyager 2, is expected to reach its own light-day in 2035.)

This incredible distance, coupled with the spacecraft's five-decade-old hardware, makes troubleshooting problems on the probe extremely arduous, Dodd explained.

An illustration depicting Voyager 1 at one light-day from Earth.

"It takes two days to diagnose anything with the spacecraft — so we can't do anything fast, and the data rates are very low," she said. "We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age."

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

According to NASA, the current glitch likely stems from Voyager's onboard computer, which is responsible for collecting data from its science instruments and transmitting it back to Earth in a readable format. The team encountered a similar problem in November 2023 that prevented Voyager 1 from sharing science data until engineers solved the issue in June 2024. The mission team is approaching this new glitch the same way they solved the previous one, NASA wrote in a blog post.

If the fix succeeds, Voyager 1 will continue transmitting data from its two remaining science instruments — a magnetometer, which measures magnetic fields in interstellar space, and a plasma wave detector, which measures charged particles in the interstellar medium. To conserve power on the aging spacecraft, the mission team shut off some of Voyager's instruments earlier this year while powering other, more efficient ones in a "Big Bang" maneuver that should keep the probe alive through at least 2027.

We are in a realm where we're going to see more anomalies with Voyager, just due to the distance and the age

However, it's only a matter of time before Voyager 1 runs out of juice and closes its mechanical eyes to the cosmos. After that, it will continue drifting through interstellar space indefinitely, carrying a Golden Record of images, music and information about life on Earth. In the meantime, Voyager will continue learning everything it can about the strange environment of the interstellar medium — the space between stars, where only Voyagers 1 and 2 have ever been before.

Voyager 1 officially reached interstellar space in 2012, after transforming our views of Jupiter, Saturn and other solar system bodies. For more about the probe's incredible discoveries, check out our collection of Voyager 1's iconic photos.

#6429. Why are the spiral arms of this galaxy glowing?

Webb’s infrared portrait of NGC 2283 reveals where young stars light up clouds of hydrogen gas in a galaxy 45 million light-years away.

Today’s Image of the Day features NGC 2283, a spiral galaxy in the constellation Canis Major.

A few bright white stars catch the eye first. Behind them, reddish clouds wind around a golden center, tracing the arms of a galaxy about 45 million light-years away.

The James Webb Space Telescope collected the data for this portrait in just 17 minutes of total exposure time.

What makes the image worth a longer look is how much is happening inside those arms.

The bright knots scattered along them show where young stars are already changing the clouds they formed from.

Elsewhere in the same galaxy, a massive star exploded in 2023, returning material to the space between stars.

The large white stars with long, sharp spikes belong to our own Milky Way.

They lie between Earth and NGC 2283 and appear in the picture because they happen to sit along Webb’s line of sight.

Their spikes come from the way light bends around parts of the telescope. Once you look past them, the galaxy’s shape is easier to pick out.

Two loosely wound arms curve away from an elongated band of stars that crosses the center.

Astronomers call that central structure a bar. Our own galaxy has one, too, but we observe the Milky Way from inside its disk.

Webb sees NGC 2283 almost face-on, giving us a clear view of how its bar and arms fit together.

Webb built this view from six exposures taken through different infrared filters.

Its Near-Infrared Camera and Mid-Infrared Instrument recorded different parts of the light coming from the same patch of sky.

Combining those observations lets astronomers see several things at once. Some filters pick up light from stars or from clouds of hydrogen energized by young stars.

Others detect the glow of carbon-rich molecules called polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, which are also found in soot on Earth.

Image processors assign visible colors to those infrared measurements.

The result lets us follow details that would otherwise be invisible to our eyes, including the uneven distribution of gas and dust along the arms.

The spiral arms look almost continuous from a distance. Look closer and they break up into bright clumps, wisps, and darker gaps.

The brightest knots include dense clouds of gas lit up by young stars.

A star begins forming when part of a cold cloud becomes dense enough to collapse under its own gravity. As material falls inward, the growing star heats up.

Some of the most massive young stars release enough ultraviolet light to energize the hydrogen around them, making the surrounding gas glow.

That glow gives astronomers a way to find places where star formation has happened recently.

In NGC 2283, the glowing clouds and young clusters make it possible to trace the arms even where dust hides some of the stars.

On January 28, 2023, astronomers discovered a supernova in NGC 2283.

Known as SN 2023AXU, it was a Type II supernova, the kind that can occur when a massive star runs out of fuel in its core.

Once the core can no longer support itself against gravity, it collapses. The resulting explosion throws the star’s outer layers into space.

Over time, material from explosions like this can mix with surrounding gas and become part of clouds that form new stars.

That process changes the ingredients available to later generations.

Elements such as oxygen and sodium can travel far from the star that released them, then end up in another star or in the material that gathers around it.

NGC 2283 is one of 55 nearby galaxies Webb observed in a program designed to study how stars, gas, and dust interact.

These galaxies are close enough for Webb to distinguish individual star clusters and gas clouds, allowing astronomers to compare conditions from one part of a galaxy to another.

In this portrait, the spiral arms may be the first thing you notice. The small knots along them are what make the scene worth coming back to.

Each marks a place where young stars are already leaving a visible imprint on the material around them.

Image Credit: ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Leroy

#6428. NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson loses reelection in North Carolina

NRCC Chairman Richard Hudson, right, here at a hearing in June, lost his reelection bid in North Carolina's 9th District. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

North Carolina Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee, has lost his race for reelection, a stinging defeat for the man charged with preserving the House majority for the GOP.

Hudson fell to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator who was leading  51 percent to 49 percent Thursday afternoon  when The Associated Press called the race in North Carolina’s 9th District.

Hudson had already conceded the race Wednesday, when it became clear that his path to victory was closing off.

“[The] voters of North Carolina’s 9th District made their choice and I respect it,” he said in a statement. “Since 2013 I’ve worked for North Carolina families. That includes the soldiers and families at Fort Bragg, who sacrifice more for this country than most people will ever know.”

Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose his seat during a midterm election this decade. In 2022, New York Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney lost reelection while serving as chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee.

Republicans across North Carolina experienced devastating losses on election night. As of Thursday afternoon, Democrats had also flipped the seats of Reps. Addison McDowell, Brad Knott and Tim Moore, as well as the open seat of retiring Rep. Chuck Edwards. The races for five other GOP-held seats remain uncalled, while Democratic Rep. Don Davis was reelected despite being targeted for defeat under a new GOP-drawn congressional map. Republicans also lost control of the North Carolina House and lost seats in the state Senate.

North Carolina’s 9th District, which includes the Eastern Piedmont region and the Fayetteville area, was far from the House battlefield for much of the midterm cycle. President Donald Trump carried the seat by 16 points in 2024, according to calculations by Inside Elections with Nathan L. Gonzales, and Hudson won a seventh term the same year by nearly 19 points. Hudson also held a financial advantage over Ojeda, raising $4.2 million to Ojeda’s $2.9 million through mid-October.

But in the waning weeks of the campaign, signs of Republican concern grew and Hudson’s campaign began spending on ads.

Ojeda was first elected to the West Virginia Senate in 2016. He ran for the U.S. House two years later as a Trump-voting Democrat but lost that race to Republican Carol Miller. He then briefly ran for the 2020 Democratic presidential nomination and also challenged GOP Sen. Shelley Moore Capito later that cycle but lost in the Democratic primary.

Ojeda moved to North Carolina in 2020, he told CityView, a local magazine, and he announced his challenge to Hudson last year.

Throughout the campaign, he attacked the incumbent over his support for Trump’s agenda, particularly the war in Iran. Ojeda is a retired Army major and the district is home to Fort Bragg, the nation’s largest Army base by population, where the Democrat was previously stationed for more than a decade.

“We did the impossible,’’ Ojeda told supporters Tuesday night. “We took on the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee, a man with political connections, the billionaire donors, and the entire Washington establishment standing beside him.”

Hudson, 55, is finishing his seventh term in the House and his second term as NRCC chair. He had no primary opponent this year and had grown used to winning reelection by comfortable margins.

As a legislator, Hudson focused much of his policy agenda on health issues such as federal pandemic preparedness programs. He serves on the House Energy and Commerce Committee and chairs the panel's Communications and Technology Subcommittee.

#6426. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Disease outbreaks revealed a weakened federal response

Outbreaks of measles, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and hantavirus exposed a weakened U.S. public health response.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

It’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” says Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

Domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” says Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in New York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

Measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

In the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy says. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy says. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

Even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, says Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and New York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy says.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

The FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”

Sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she said they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the New York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, says Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”

Starting in 2027, FDA plans to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, says Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

“We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”

When the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

Confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered

As cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of new Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli says.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

Nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond quickly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli says.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

The United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” says Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”

Instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the New York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm says. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm says. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”

The international collaboration had some successes, says virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in New York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

Hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a new one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

“We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become important,” Palacios says. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”

Recently, Live Science asked its readers which animal they'd want to communicate with, based on a new study that leveraged AI to decode different vocalizations of zebra finches.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Recently, University of California, Berkeley ethologist Julie Elie used artificial intelligence (AI) and behavioral experiments to decode the different vocalizations of zebra finches (Taeniopygia guttata), bringing scientists one step closer to talking to animals.

Birds are just some of many animals that experts hope to understand and communicate with. Scientists are also deciphering the clicks and calls of sperm whales and humpback whales. Some animals, like cats, can change their meows depending on what they're seeking from their owners, such as food or attention.

In the wake of Elie's new findings, Live Science asked its readers what animal they would want to talk to if they could.

Over 550 people voted in our poll, with 54% picking dog. The next-largest voting group, 28% of respondents, chose cat.

The comments reflected the obvious trend of readers wanting to speak to their pets. One commenter wrote, "Cats, simply because I've had more of them as pets over the decades than anything else. I don't think spiders would be interesting conversationalists, I'm unlikely to encounter whales here in the middle of North America, and dogs that I meet on my daily walks are only invested in the canine treats I carry."

Another reader said we'd never be able to understand our pets even if we could communicate with them. "Unfortunately you would have to experience the world through your nose to truly understand what they experience. To understand what a dog is thinking you would have to 'be' a dog. A problem with communicating with any non-human being, whether it be octopi, whale, cat or extra terrestrial. It seems to be a human thing that people can't just sit, observe and interpret the world around them as it is. Everything needs to be explained!"

Not everyone chose cats and dogs, though. One reader wrote, "I would want to know my horse's backstory."

Several other commenters mentioned octopuses, with one commenter saying, "I’m disappointed that octopi weren't included on the list. I've read that they are incredibly intelligent, interact with humans and are able to think and plan. Also they can shape shift and change color and patterns. I love my dogs but I don't imagine they are capable of matching the observations and conversations octopi might have."

Do you agree or disagree with these readers? Let us know in the comments!

#6424. The 8 Best Portable Air Conditioners for When You Don’t Want to Install a Window Unit

Prepare for easy setup, effective cooling, and the ability to move from room to room.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Unlike window air conditioners, portable air conditioners roll easily from room to room and take only minutes to set up—no brackets, no tools, no sweating through a complicated installation before you can start sweating less. Most just require a nearby window and wall outlet to get cold air flowing. Yes, they tend to cost a bit more than window units, but the tradeoff is real: you can’t beat the convenience their portability adds, which is why many people choose them over other models. Plus your view isn’t blocked by a giant metal box.

Portable air conditioners have an internal fan that moves hot, humid air over a refrigerant-gas-filled coil to cool and expel it into a room to lower the temperature. The moisture it strips from the air collects in an internal reservoir that you’ll periodically need to drain. Higher-end units either pump it out automatically or evaporate it entirely so you never have to think about it. Because the whole unit rolls on casters, you can take the cold air with you instead of running more energy intensive central a/c or buying multiple window units.

To find the best models to recommend, we tested air conditioners from trusted brands like LG, GE, Black + Decker, Midea, Hisense, and more. These are the units that stood out and are worth the investment.

We placed each unit in its own room and directed its discharge hose to the outside, then set the appliance’s temperature to 68 degrees and its fan speed to maximum. We directed the cold air each unit discharged at a target 8 feet away, then used an infrared thermometer to measure the temperature at four different locations on the target. We also checked the appliance’s outlet to see if it maintained a consistent temperature. To test the wheels’ durability and noise, we rolled each unit on a hard surface to maximize squeaks and rattles.

We also sent several air conditioners to our staff’s homes and apartments for further testing, where our editors used them over the course of weeks within the living spaces. We tested how easy they were to use, how they operated over time, and how easy they were to integrate into daily life.

For our most recent update, we identified the most trusted brands and surveyed current models across a range of price points, BTU capacities, and capabilities, making sure we had options for small rooms and larger ones. From there, we narrowed the field by prioritizing units with strong efficiency ratings, straightforward setup, and drainage designs that won’t require constant attention.

Our top-rated portable air conditioner stands out for how quickly it cools down a room. During testing, we turned it on and almost immediately began feeling a cold blast of air with very little runtime. The a/c noticeably brought down the temperature in just a few minutes, plus it did so quietly. According to LG, the unit operates at just 44 decibels on its lowest setting.

The unit has three modes: cooling, fan, and dry. Cooling and fan are pretty straightforward while dry actually turns the unit into a dehumidifier. So, when you don’t actively need it, feel free to have it run in moist spaces like your laundry room or garage.

The louvers on the a/c unit can be set to move up and down on their own. This actually made a pretty notable difference in full-room air circulation and helped get rid of hot air that sat near the ceiling.

Setup was also quite easy, as the air conditioner was almost fully assembled right out of the box. Even connecting the hose and slider into the window was intuitive and took less than 5 minutes total. With the four wheels and very basic setup, we were rolling it from room to room in no time.

If you’re hesitant to spend over $500 on a portable air conditioning unit, this option from Dreo is the best bang for your buck. Considering the relatively low price, its power and added features surprised us during testing.

First and foremost, the unit blasts cold air quite quickly. In fact, it worked nearly as well as several of the more expensive units we tested. The window exhaust has a foam seal to make sure no hot exhaust or exterior air sneaks in.

The air conditioner pairs with Dreo’s app for connection and precise programming, however we ended up using (and loving) the physical remote. It has 10 buttons for changing the speed and temperature, setting the air mode, operating the sleep timer, turning on the auto-swing louver function, and more. Plus, there’s an attached magnet for convent storage on top of the unit.

On the front of the unit there are manual controls and a digital display that shows the room temperature, mode, and fan power. So whether you’re using the remote, app, or changing settings manually, you know exactly what the status is.

Full Dreo AC515S Portable Air Conditioner Review

This Whynter’s amperage and BTU capacity position it firmly in the heavy-duty cooling category. The same applies to its dehumidifying power, with the unit capturing up to 71 pints of moisture per day. The biggest downside is that it’s also firmly in the heavy category, weighing over 70 pounds.

The portable air conditioner has a dual-hose design (intake and exhaust) for reducing the amount of condensate that the a/c collects, since it’s supposed to be removed in the exhaust air stream.

A similar model (ARC-14SH) also operates in heat pump/heater mode. For a slightly smaller model, check out the Whynter Elite ARC-122DS below.

While most units are either quiet or powerful, the GE Profile Portable A/C offers a bit of both worlds. Because of its dual-hose design, the air conditioner takes in air at a much higher rate than one that relies on the body of the unit to do this work. With more air coming in, more cold air comes out. This was definitely true during testing.

On its average setting, the a/c noticeably cooled down a mid-sized room in less than ten minutes. Holding up my hand to the vents, I felt a cold blast of air much stronger than other options I tried out. Going even further, the Profile has a turbo mode that turns the fans up to an even higher level.

The effectiveness of the cooling has do to with more than just airflow, too. This portable a/c unit also comes with auto louvers that more evenly distribute cold air by shifting the vents up and down. I particularly like this feature for apartments like mine which are a few floors up and end up with a lot of accumulated hot air near the ceiling. The auto louvers help bring down the temperature of the entire room down as opposed to just blasting cold air in one direction.

While all these features impressed me, the unit’s best quality is that it doesn’t stand out at all. This a/c is incredibly quiet. While I barely noticed the sound at normal levels, when I set the unit to quiet mode, the noise levels drop to a whisper. According to GE, quiet mode is measured at just 42 decibels, which is lower than all other options we recommend.

This makes the Profile an ideal choice for overnight use or in small rooms. However, the remote control buttons don’t light up, so if you’re using it at night, you may need a flashlight, phone, or bedside lamp.

Full GE Profile Portable Air Conditioner Review

If the other units on this list take up more real estate than you have or want to give, the Dreo AC319S is the one you won’t have to make room for. It's the most compact refrigerant-based portable air conditioner we've included—at just over 17 inches wide and 28 inches tall, it slips into corners and tight apartments where bulkier units don't fit. Be warned, though, the tradeoff for that smaller footprint is smaller cooling coverage. This one is best for bedrooms, home offices, and other spaces up to 300 square feet.

But what it gives up in cooling-size capabilities, it makes up for in smart features and low maintenance. The drainage-free system, powered by Dreo's patented internal pump and dual water sensors, handles condensation automatically. In moderately humid conditions, you'll likely never need to drain the unit at all. The Dreo app sends a notification if the tank does fill up, which is a thoughtful touch. That kind of hands-off convenience is why this one made our list.

At just 45 decibels on its lowest setting, it's whisper-quiet on par with the priciest units here. Smart controls are also unusually comprehensive. In addition to Alexa and Google Assistant, the AC319S works with Siri, making it one of the only portable ACs that pairs nicely with Apple products. The circular LED display looks sharp, though you can’t dim it, so keep that in mind if you plan to use it overnight in rooms you want to stay dark.

If you’re fortunate to have a large living room, an open-plan studio, or a finished basement, you know the luxury of size comes with a cost—cooling oversized areas can be tough. To beat the heat in big rooms, the Whynter ARC-1230WN is the unit we’d point you toward.

With 14,000 BTUs, it covers up to 600 square feet—more than any other unit on this list. In independent testing, it dropped room temperature by about 12 degrees in a single hour, a result no other unit came close to matching.

A big part of that performance comes from Whynter's hose-in-hose dual-hose design. Unlike a standard dual-hose setup, the intake and exhaust lines run concentrically inside a single tube, preventing heat leakage between the airstreams and improving overall efficiency. The inverter compressor, which ramps up and down rather than cycling on and off, keeps noise down once the room reaches your set temperature and reduces energy use.

According to Whynter, the inverter technology delivers 20 percent more cooling capacity and over 40 percent energy savings compared to non-inverter models. Do note, though, that while this is technically a portable unit, at more than 75 pounds, it’s one you’ll want to set up for the season, not haul around on the regular.

If you're shopping for a portable AC because you have a room your HVAC system can’t handle, the Midea Duo MAP14HS1TBL is our top recommendation. It's a four-season unit: the same inverter-driven, hose-in-hose dual-hose design that makes it such an effective cooler works equally well in heat mode, and switching between the two is as easy as a click on the remote or SmartHome app—no setup or adjustments required.

The dual-hose design pulls in fresh air and expels exhaust air through a single concentric hose, keeping a neutral pressure balance in rooms. This prevents warm outside air from coming back in through gaps and cracks. Midea's airflow system also projects air up to 26 feet, which makes a real difference in longer rooms where less forceful units only cool the area immediately around them.

We’re also impressed by the smart controls. The SmartHome app works on iOS, Android, and Apple Watch, and voice control is compatible with Alexa and Google Assistant. I also like that you can completely turn off the control panel lights, which is a sleep-saving feature for overnight use. And at 42 decibels on its lowest setting, it's among the quietest options we’ve come across.

We were pleasantly surprised by the power and value offered by this small portable air conditioner from Black+Decker. It begins producing cold air very quickly, though not quite at the volume of many other air conditioners we tested. That said, it still reduced the temperature of its target at a rapid rate.

The unit provides multiple fan speeds, dedicated dehumidification, a timer setting, and a sleep setting. Note that there is no heater setting on this appliance. It’s meant to cool and dehumidify exclusively.

Reviews Editor Amber Joglar tested out the four-in-one version of this model which also functions as a heater. After just 10 minutes of use in her room, Joglar felt, “a noticeable shift in the air temperature.”

The quick cooldown times stood out across both models, though Joglar also pointed out that this led to the exhaust pipes heating up quickly as well. This isn’t necessarily a problem, but if you plan on using the unit for several hours a day, consider covering the tubes in insulation.

In addition to the cold air, Joglar liked the remote and LED control panel, saying, “I normally just change settings on the air conditioner itself because it’s right next to my bed, so backlit controls are helpful.”

Similarly, the remote control is great for when she’s already in bed or wants to pre-cool the room before she’s ready to go to sleep.

Joglar’s model also heats rooms. So, instead of storing it in a closet or attic for the cold winter months, she simply switches functionality.

Read Our Full Black+Decker Portable Air Conditioner Review

Coverage area is one of the most important factors in choosing an air conditioner. Manufacturers rate units in square footage, but that number assumes an average ceiling height (roughly eight feet) and room insulation. If the room is especially hot in the summer (for example, it’s a finished attic or it has large, south-facing windows) we recommend bumping up to the next size rather than buying a unit that will run constantly and struggle to keep up.

An air conditioner’s cooling capacity is typically measured in British Thermal Units, or BTU, per hour. To gauge coverage, figure roughly 20 BTU per square foot of space. Most portable a/c units range from 5,000 to 20,000 BTUs, which puts their effective range roughly between 350 and 700 square feet. So when in doubt, size up—an oversized unit cycles off when it hits your target temperature, while an undersized one never stops trying.

Single-hose units essentially recirculate the room’s air to cool it and have one line that runs outdoors to expel exhaust. The catch is that expelling air creates a slight negative pressure in the room, which pulls in warm air from other parts of the house and from outside through gaps around doors and windows. It works, but it’s working against itself.

Dual-hose units solve this by pulling outside air in through one hose for cooling and pushing hot exhaust out through a second hose. The result is a more self-contained system that’s noticeably more efficient, especially in larger spaces. The tradeoff is price.

Because dual-hose models are more complex, they tend to be more expensive. If you only have a small space to cool, a portable a/c with a single hose may suit your needs just fine. For anything larger, the dual-hose design is worth seriously considering.

Hose length determines how far away from a window you can maneuver your portable air conditioner. If you set it up in a large room, or one where the nearest window is far from where most people gather, hose length becomes more important.

It also plays a key role in room setup. If the hose isn’t long enough to set the air conditioner in front of large furniture pieces, you may have to rearrange the room for the most effective cooling. Most hoses range anywhere from 50 to 90 inches fully extended. This should give you enough space to make adjustments and pull the air conditioner closer to the center of the room if needed.

Most portable air conditioners hover between 50 and 60 decibels while they’re running—that’s roughly the noise level of a normal conversation. In most cases, that’s fine during the day, but if you’re planning to run the unit in a bedroom overnight, those numbers start to matter.

Units that dip below 50 decibels in their quietest modes are on par with most ceiling fans and are easier to sleep through; a few on this list get impressively close to whisper-quiet. Pay attention to the decibel rating at the unit’s lowest fan setting, not just its average operating level.

Much like larger ductless mini-split air conditioners, some portable air conditioners include a heat pump. “If you’re shopping for an a/c unit because you have a space not currently cooled or heated, one of these models may warrant consideration,” says gear editor Bradley Ford. “Similarly, you may have a room that your HVAC system doesn’t reach effectively. Rooms like this are typically either too cold or hot, depending on the season. If this is the case, a unit with heating capabilities may be able to fill your HVAC gap.”

Every portable a/c pulls moisture out of the air, similar to home dehumidifiers. The question is what happens to it next. Budget units collect it in an internal pan that you’ll need to manually drain, sometimes daily in humid conditions.

Other units use self-evaporating technology to push moisture out through the exhaust hose with no bucket to remember. A few high-end models go even further, offering a continuous drainage port where you can attach a hose and never think about water again. If low-maintenance matters to you, the drainage method is a factor to consider.

There isn’t a clear superior option between window units and portable options. Choosing between the two largely depends on your home, windows, and personal needs. That said, window air conditioning units are generally faster at bringing temperatures down and run more efficiently than their portable counterparts.

Portable air conditioners have certainly closed the gap over time in terms of cooling ability, but still lag behind if that’s your number one priority.

Portable units stand out because of their convenience and ease of setup. If you don’t have compatible windows, get a portable unit. If you need quick cooling in a spot that generally doesn’t need air conditioning, get a portable unit. If you want just one machine for your entire apartment, get a portable unit.

Portable air conditioners are compatible with a lot more window openings than window units, so you can use them regardless of your apartment or home fixtures.

New portable a/c units are relatively energy efficient across the board. That said, it’s certainly a sliding scale. There are several ways in which energy efficiency is calculated for air conditioners, but the shorthand is if your a/c unit is Energy Star-certified, it’s worth getting.

For items that don’t have Energy Star certification, pay attention to the CEER, EER, and SEER numbers. In short, look for an air conditioner with a CEER above 10, with anything above 12 qualifying for Energy Star certification. Similarly, look out for a SEER above 14 in the north and 15 in the south as well as an EER above 10. These are general numbers, but serve as a basic guide when choosing between different options.

One of the biggest issues to solve with portable air conditioners is cooling efficiency. While most units generate a ton of cold air, leakage from the hose or exhaust port can work against that. There are two key things you can do: insulate the opening in the window and insulate the hose itself.

Many portable units provide foam pieces that fit in and around the window insert to minimize the amount of hot air that leaks in from outside. The hose itself won’t come with foam insulation pieces, but you can perform a similar trick by buying one online or by making one yourself. Some people use blankets while others have used everything from reflective sun shades to Amazon plastic packaging. The goal is to prevent heat from the tube from radiating into your living space.
