#6423. At the Races: After the deluge

Tuesday’s rout by Democrats has led one group dedicated to electing more Republican women to Congress to warn of a “crisis-level decline” of female GOP members on Capitol Hill.

Danielle Barrow, the president of Women for Women Action Fund, drew parallels between this week’s results and the 2018 blue wave.

“After 2018, when Republicans lost 40 seats and elected only one new Republican woman, the party made a real commitment to recruiting and investing in women – and it worked,” Barrow said in a statement Wednesday, adding that women accounted for 11 of the 15 House seats the GOP picked up in the 2020 election. But she cautioned that the party needs to sustain that focus across election cycles.

“Republicans cannot only make this investment after a wipeout election and abandon it when things improve,” she said. “It is time for party leaders to treat this as a permanent strategy, not a crisis response.”

The ranks of House Republican women won’t plummet to as low as after the 2018 elections, when the caucus had just 13 female members. At least 18 Republican women have won House races so far, according to The Associated Press, and two others are leading as of Thursday afternoon. The conference is likely to see two new female members: Florida’s Sydney Gruters, the wife of RNC Chairman Joe Gruters, and Washington state’s Amanda McKinney, who holds a comfortable lead as votes continue to be counted.

Still, those figures are worlds apart from House Democrats, whose caucus will have more than 100 women next year.

“We have always known that when women run, women win,” Florida Rep. Lois Frankel, chair of the member-led Elect Democratic Women PAC, said in a statement Wednesday.

Those incoming new members span the ideological range of the party, including progressives from New York and California who scored big primary wins this summer, to more moderate Democrats who flipped seats in Virginia and Pennsylvania.

House Democrats had set a public goal this cycle to push their female membership past 100. Former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who is retiring at the end of the year, said electing Democratic women had been her “passion” since she joined the House in 1987.

“We made a decision to make more room for women at the tables of power – and generations of candidates, organizers and supporters have carried that work forward,” she said.

Blue breakthrough: Democrats flipped the House and Senate this week, giving the party one of its biggest nights in decades. On the Senate side, they wrested seats from Republicans in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas, Iowa, North Carolina and Ohio, while finally flipping Maine. Meanwhile, on the House side, Democrats were on track to not just win every race rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections but also pick up seats in deep-red territory that weren’t considered competitive until late in the cycle. Mary Ellen and Daniela summed up their initial election night takeaways, including how Democratic moderates and progressives both cheered the results and why many of Trump’s picks flopped at the ballot box.

Not going anywhere: The top Senate Democrat, Charles E. Schumer of New York, is confident he will be elected majority leader by his caucus, especially after the party’s resounding midterm wins. Several of his incoming members have promised to support others, our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports, but the reality is there’s no real plausible alternative. Schumer’s own seat is up in 2028.

Redistricting rout: Republicans’ redistricting gambit hasn’t paid off as they’d hoped, the latest election results show, with the GOP appearing poised to flip only a handful of redrawn seats. Democratic incumbents who sought reelection from their reconfigured seats appeared poised to all win, although the race for Rep. Darren Soto’s Central Florida seat remained uncalled as of Thursday afternoon.

Taking the chair: Among the bruising defeats that North Carolina Republicans suffered this week was National Republican Congressional Committee Chairman Richard Hudson’s loss to Democrat Richard Ojeda, a former West Virginia state senator. Hudson is now the second party campaign chief to lose reelection this decade after New York’s Sean Patrick Maloney , who lost in 2022 while serving as the DCCC chair.

New senators: The incoming Senate Democratic class includes a returning senator, a former governor, two lieutenant governors and a congressman, a notable amount of governing experience. Meanwhile, five Republican House members are moving across the Rotunda after winning open Senate seats.

Member-to-governor pipeline grows: Five newly elected governors will be departing Capitol Hill to become the top executive of their state or territory, Savannah reports. Additionally, two former members who also served in the Biden administration were elected governor, though a trio of House Republicans fell short in their gubernatorial bids.

Comeback season: Roll Call’s Nick Eskow reports on the former members who are poised to return to the House or Senate next year, with at least seven winning comeback bids Tuesday.

The firsts: Several candidates made history this week with their elections to Congress or the governorships of their state. Roll Call’s Andrew Menezes rounds up the milestone wins.

D.C. in the House: Robert White, D.C.’s newly elected nonvoting delegate, told our colleague Nina Heller that he plans to lobby fellow Democrats next year to support D.C. statehood. A potential selling point: The party could tackle affordability concerns better with two Democratic senators from the deep-blue District, he said.

Keeping count: As of 4:30 p.m. Thursday, Democrats had flipped 42 seats in the House and seven in the Senate, according to the AP. Republicans have so far picked up two House seats, both through redistricting. Twenty-eight House contests and two Senate races (Alaska and Mississippi) remain uncalled as of publication time. Check out Roll Call’s results tracker for updates as the races are called.

Indie losses: Independent Senate hopefuls running in deep-red states did not find success on Tuesday, even in races without a Democrat on the ballot. In Nebraska, former union leader Dan Osborn came up short in his second Senate bid. In Idaho, former state legislator Todd Achilles failed to dislodge Sen. Jim Risch, while Navy veteran Brian Bengs couldn’t topple South Dakota Sen. Mike Rounds. In Montana, where the Democratic nominee did not drop out, former university president Seth Bodnar lost to Republican Kurt Alme. On the House side, Alaska GOP Rep. Nick Begich comfortably leads commercial fisherman Bill Hill, though below the 50 percent threshold needed to avoid a ranked-choice runoff. With votes still being counted, the AP had yet to call the race at publication time.

Not just Congress: The blue wave that broke Republican majorities on Capitol Hill also washed over state legislatures. Democrats are poised to hold new majorities in 12 legislative chambers, including the North Carolina House and Texas House, according to the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, although some results aren’t official yet. The party also won governing trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Meanwhile, in blue states, Democrats tightened their grip on government: In Rhode Island, Republicans are on track to hold just 10 seats in the entire 113-member legislature, while next door in Connecticut, the 36-seat Senate could have as few as three GOP members.

Blame game: As Republicans take stock of what went wrong for them in the midterms, Vice President JD Vance was quick to point to the Iran conflict as an insurmountable albatross. “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance said in a lengthy X post. “If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. … But everyone knows why we lost.”

But the tariffs: A pair of Republican former senators, Arizona’s Jeff Flake and Pennsylvania’s Patrick J. Toomey, both also urged their party to focus on the impact of Trump’s tariff policies. “Arbitrary and capricious tariffs directly raised costs for all American consumers,” Toomey wrote Wednesday on X. “Many voted for Democrats yesterday.”

Staying put: Pennsylvania Rep. Brendan F. Boyle says he will remain in the House, where he’s poised to become the next Budget Committee chair, rather than launch a Democratic primary challenge to Sen. John Fetterman next cycle.

Bayh Bayh Bayh: A third generation of Indiana’s famed Bayh family won political office this week, with Beau Bayh’s election as secretary of state. Bayh, a Marine Corps veteran, follows in the footsteps of his father, Evan Bayh, who won the same post 40 years ago before going on to serve as governor and senator, and his late grandfather, Birch Bayh, who won three terms in the Senate. Indiana Democrats had a breakthrough election this week, defeating GOP Rep. Victoria Spartz, winning a second statewide office, unseating the speaker and breaking the GOP supermajority in the state House.

A win and a loss: Nebraska Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts won reelection, but his wife, Democrat Susanne Shore, lost a special election for a seat on University of Nebraska Board of Regents, which governs the university system. Shore, who lost to a fellow Democrat in the officially nonpartisan race, was making her first bid for elective office.

Bans on the ballot: Voters in Arizona, Nebraska and Washington state have approved new measures barring transgender athletes from participating in girls sports. A similar proposal in Colorado also appears likely to pass, although the AP had yet to call it as of publication time.

Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections shares 15 initial lessons from the midterm elections, from the president’s “political mortality” to candidate quality and the power of personal brands. And, Nathan writes, as bad a night as it was for Republicans, it could have been even worse.

As Maine goes: The New York Times caught up with with Republican Sen. Susan Collins, who lost her bid for a sixth term in Maine. Collins, who had survived tough cycles before, spoke of getting “caught up in the Trump tsunami” and how she finally had her “Margaret Chase Smith moment.”

“These are extinction-level numbers”: Texas Monthly sat down for an interview with former state House Speaker Dade Phelan, who anticipated a down-ballot GOP rout but not the full extent of it. “MAGA needs to be dead,’’ said the Republican, who led the push to impeach state Attorney General Ken Paxton in 2023 and then was targeted for defeat by Trump. He opted against reelection this year.

Corruption a top issue: The Associated Press reported that its 2026 voter poll found corruption at the top of the list of concerns for voters who helped sweep Democrats into power on Capitol Hill.

Tar Heeled: Among the states where Republicans suffered their biggest defeats Tuesday, perhaps none was more stunning than North Carolina, where they've so far lost five U.S. House seats and are trailing in one another and lost control of the state House. The (Raleigh) News & Observer looks at how maps “designed to deliver strong Republican majorities [failed] so spectacularly at that goal.”

Support and discord: Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s sharply critical views toward Israel roiled the Jewish community in Michigan. But exit polling suggests most Jewish voters backed him, albeit in smaller numbers than they might have had a different Democrat run, Religion News Service reports.

That's how many House districts won by Trump in 2024 have been called for Democratic candidates by the AP as of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time on Thursday.

Twenty-eight additional Trump-won districts remain uncalled at publication time, and Democrats are currently leading in eight of those races.

The figures stand in sharp contrast to the start of the cycle, when there were just 13 House Democrats in districts that backed Trump in 2024.

Since then, several Republican-led states redrew their congressional maps in an effort to increase the number of Trump-won districts and improve their party’s chances of holding the House.

In large part, this effort appears to have backfired in 2026, with the Democratic wave cresting high enough to wash over dozens of Trump-won districts. Twenty-one of the 52 Democratic wins so far have come in states that redrew their congressional lines: Texas (six Trump-won seats), North Carolina (six), Ohio (five), Florida (three) and Alabama (one).

Congressional Republicans are holding leadership elections next week as they transition from the majority to the minority party. Speaker Mike Johnson is not seeking his conference’s top post, setting up a clash to be the next House minority leader. On the Senate side, South Dakota’s John Thune hopes to continue leading his party in the chamber.

#6422. Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A star called “Little Bao” danced with its giant partner “Big Bao”

An image captured by NASA’s Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) telescope shows the Andromeda galaxy, which is the closest large galaxy to our Milky Way — and the home galaxy of Big and Little Bao.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

For seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

In work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.)

First, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Big Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

Still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar says, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”

In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For the first time, physicists have used quantum entanglement to verify a person's physical location. That could one day make it much harder for hackers to pretend to be somewhere they're not, the team says.

In the new study, published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature, researchers at the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) used pairs of entangled photons (particles of light) to confirm that a participant was at a specific spot between two stations on NIST's campus in Boulder, Colorado. The method is called quantum position verification, and this is the first complete demonstration of it.

If the technology matures, it could help protect health records, stop remote attackers from sending commands to power grids or water treatment plants, block unauthorized stock trades and thwart phishing attacks carried out over phone or video calls, according to a statement.

"It's a totally new application for quantum networks," Shalm said. "You can add another layer of security to these systems that anchors a lot of this digital security to a position."

Location is a basic layer of security. Banks, power grids and government agencies often limit access to sensitive systems to people who are physically inside a secure building. But classical (nonquantum) ways of proving location remotely, which time how long signals take to travel, can be spoofed by hackers working together. Quantum physics can close that security gap, because a single quantum particle can't be copied.

"Is this call coming from my bank, or is it coming from someone in North Korea or somewhere else?" Krister Shalm, a quantum physicist at NIST who led the team, told Live Science. "That's really powerful if you can anchor digital security to a physical location."

In the experiment, the team used a technique called ranging, which is similar to the principles behind echolocation, radar and the lidar sensors found in some smartphones. It sends a signal and measures how long it takes for the response to return.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"You can send a signal at the speed of light and measure how long it takes to get back," Shalm told Live Science. "But the problem is, that's the thing that can always be spoofed classically."

In the experiment, two trusted stations called "verifiers" sat 640 feet (195 meters) apart, linked by cables and optical fibers running through the hallways of a NIST research building. A "prover," whose location the verifiers wanted to confirm, sat in between.

One verifier created pairs of entangled photons — particles so deeply linked that measuring one reveals something about the other, even when they're separated at great distances. The verifier kept one photon from each pair and sent its twin to the prover. At the same time, both verifiers sent random bits of information that were timed to reach the prover at the same moment.

The prover combined the two inputs with a simple math operation and used the result to decide how to measure the photon's polarization ‪—‬ the direction in which its electric field oscillates. The measuring device works much like the filter in polarized sunglasses. A detector then recorded whether the photon made it through the filter, and the prover sent that yes-or-no result back to both verifiers.

Because nothing travels faster than light, the round-trip time told the verifiers how far away the prover could be. And because the photon can't be copied, the measurement had to be made in that exact spot.

To confirm that no one cheated, the team ran a loophole-free Bell test, which checks whether particles are more strongly correlated than classical physics allows. If anyone tampers with the photons or the equipment, the test fails. Shalm led one of the first such tests in 2015.

NIST physicist Krister Shalm performing a Bell test in 2015. Shalm was part of the team that demonstrated the new location verification method.

Scientists first proposed position verification in the late 2000s, but the experiments are extremely demanding, Shalm said. Many earlier designs could tolerate losing only a few percent of the photons along the way, which is "just not practical or reasonable" with today's technology. The NIST team relied on superconducting detectors that catch nearly every photon.

The surprise, Shalm said, was that the Bell test approach worked at all on the first try. It offers the strongest security of any quantum protocol because it makes very few assumptions about how the equipment works, but it is usually the hardest to pull off. "The sort of gold-plated deluxe version — you were able to do that on the first demonstration of a full protocol," he said.

The system ran about 250,000 trials per second. Each verification required 30 million to 60 million rounds of signals sent back and forth ‪—‬ roughly two to four minutes of data. Over two days in fall 2024, the team ran 335 verifications, and nearly all of them passed. The prover's location was confirmed within a region about 4.5 times smaller in volume than what a comparable classical method could guarantee, the team said.

The experiment proved secure against attackers who shared little or no entanglement of their own. Protecting against attackers with more powerful quantum resources will require longer strings of random bits, the researchers wrote.

The initial users of this technology are expected to be data centers, financial backend systems and critical infrastructure like power plants, Shalm said. However, incorporating this technology into cellphones will take significantly longer, as the components are currently too large and expensive.

"In terms of a computer analogy, we are much closer to the building-sized computers of the 1950s and 1960s than today's smartphones," he said in an email. "However, with consistent improvement it might be possible in several decades to come up with a compact handheld version of the devices needed for quantum position verification."

Real-world use may be more than a decade away, Scott Glancy, a NIST physicist and study co-author, said in the statement. To verify that a customer is truly communicating with someone from their bank, high-quality quantum networks must be utilized to share entangled photons between the two parties.

The team already knows how to speed things up. Faster measurement devices could cut each verification from minutes to about a second, according to the study, and low-latency communication links could shrink the verified zone to a single building, even with stations miles apart.

"It may not be this year, but I think it's something that we're building towards, and we know the steps that are needed to get there," Shalm said.

Kavuri, G. A., Zhang, Y., Gookin, A. R., Patra, S., Bienfang, J. C., Fu, H., Alnawakhtha, Y., Reddy, D., V., Mazurek, M. D., Abellán, C., Amaya, W., Mitchell, M. W., Miller, C. A., Mirin, R. P., Stevens, M. J., Glancy, S., Knill, E., & Shalm, L. K. (2026). Quantum position verification with remote untrusted devices. Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11247-3

#6419. As Democrats look to next era, the veto and the filibuster await

Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer greets House Minority Whip Katherine Clark at the Center for American Progress Action Fund’s “Results to Roadmap” event on Thursday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

As Democrats continue their victory lap after their big wins on election night, outside groups and incoming freshmen are already turning up the pressure — and laying out competing visions of what the next two years should look like.

For Senate Democratic leader Charles E. Schumer, it bears repeating that “the Democrats aren’t all exactly the same.”

“The most important lesson of this whole election, and one we all need to internalize if we’re going to truly build a durable majority, is populism and moderation are not mutually exclusive,” he said at a Center for American Progress Action Fund event on Thursday.

Voters are expecting results as Democrats claim a mandate to address costs and corruption. “Our majority will be measured against one test and one test only: Have we made your life better?” Schumer said.

He acknowledged, however, that their plans could run into a President Donald Trump-sized wall: the presidential veto.

“Will everything pass? Will Trump sign all of it into law? Knowing Trump’s and Republicans’  intransigence, of course not. But I will promise the American people: The Democratic Party will fight to make your life more affordable, your government more competent, your capital less corrupt, bill by bill, brick by brick, for as long as it takes for you to feel the difference,” Schumer said, hinting the road could be a long one.

But several progressive lawmakers and groups say the next Congress cannot be business as usual.

Indivisible, a progressive political organization that has described the Trump administration as a “fascistic clown show,” sent a memo to Senate Democratic offices Thursday morning urging them not to “squander” their momentum and to “fight at a level that matches the public’s demand for action.”

“Who leads the party in this era must be an open question, not a coronation. It’s time to define what the next era of the Democratic Party will be,” the memo reads.

The group has been encouraging voters to speak up and demand their senators hold “a contested leadership election, not a cleared field for Schumer.”

Meanwhile, Schumer has projected confidence he will keep his spot atop the caucus, especially after he helped pave the way for Tuesday’s blue wave. “I’ll be reelected as majority leader,” he said Wednesday. But the pressure campaign points to some tough math and harsh realities for the top Democrat — including some that mirror the woes of the outgoing Republican Majority Leader John Thune.

Among the demands outlined by Indivisible is one with a troubled recent history: “Breaking the filibuster on the first day of the new session.”

Democrats need to leverage “every procedural tool” if they “want the public to believe their campaign promises weren’t just more talk from politicians who are just like the old politicians they hated,” the memo reads.

The group isn’t alone in floating a new approach to the chamber’s 60-vote threshold for invoking cloture and ending debate. Some current and incoming lawmakers have signaled they would be open to going “nuclear” and abolishing the legislative filibuster, following in the footsteps of past majorities in both parties who have similarly changed how other Senate business is handled, like judicial nominees.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., argued in an op-ed in Time this week that Democrats could in some cases use existing tools, like a party-line process known as budget reconciliation, to pass their priorities. For non-budget items, like “bills to ban stock trading by federal officials or crack down on Trump’s corruption in plain sight,” Democrats should start by putting them up for a vote on the floor and letting “Republicans decide if they want to stay tied to such corruption.”

“And, if they do, then let’s clear away Senate filibuster rules and pass the laws anyway,” she wrote.

Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas told NBC News on Monday ahead of his victory, “I believe the majority has the right to govern in this country, and the filibuster, which is not in the Constitution and is a Jim Crow relic, is leading to gridlock in our nation’s capital.”

Schumer ignored a question about nuking the filibuster at Wednesday’s event, saying instead, “The first thing we’ll do is reduce costs and work the legislative process.”

It would take 51 votes in the Senate for Democrats to go “nuclear” and establish a new precedent, a math problem that Thune knows all too well. The Republican from South Dakota faced loud criticism from conservatives online and hard-liners in his own party who said he wasn’t doing enough to try to pass a sprawling voter ID bill known as the SAVE America Act. But Thune repeatedly insisted he didn’t have the votes to change the chamber’s filibuster rules.

Many senators fear that blowing up the 60-vote threshold would fundamentally change the role of the Senate and its ability to tap the brakes on legislation that doesn’t have durable bipartisan support. Democrats went through a similar debate over the filibuster in 2022, during Schumer's first stint as majority leader. Even as others in their party pushed to pass sweeping voting rights legislation by any means necessary, Kyrsten Sinema and Joe Manchin, then moderate Democratic senators, held firm against filibuster changes.

And Schumer will have at least one Democrat on his hands who has already spoken up in defense of the filibuster, reversing his previous position. “I now recognize how important the filibuster is and the state our country would be in without it,” Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania wrote in a Washington Post op-ed earlier this summer, praising Sinema and Manchin as “courageous” holdouts who were wrongly “vilified” for holding the line.

None of that points to an easy ride for the incoming Democratic majority leader. And if fights over the filibuster weren’t enough, the caucus is also bracing for a different kind of intraparty angst, this time over impeachment.

The next likely House Judiciary Committee chairman, Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., told reporters on Thursday: “I have not had a single member of Congress or even a candidate say we’ve got to start out by impeaching Donald Trump.”

“For us, impeachment is not a fetish. It’s certainly not a taboo. We’ve impeached the guy twice,” he said, referring to Democrats’ efforts during the first Trump administration. “The problem has been over on the Senate side, and for us, it is a tool in the constitutional toolkit.”

Even if the House were to impeach Trump, a conviction would require a two-thirds supermajority vote in the Senate. And some Democrats are eager not to waste their hard-earned political capital on an impeachment quest that could alienate moderate voters and do nothing to bring down costs for everyday Americans.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, who boosted candidates in battleground races and recently released a roadmap for the new Congress, said at the CAP event on Thursday that lawmakers should “hold oversight hearings and expose the corruption of this administration. I’m not suggesting that that necessarily leads to impeachment. Maybe it does.”

Sounding more certain for Democrats in both chambers is their desire to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth over the war in Iran.

But that could be dealt with in the lame duck if Rep. Thomas Massie’s, R-Ky., resolution prevails next week. His proposal includes eight articles of impeachment, including allegations that Hegseth violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in his prosecution of the Iran war and acted illegally in military campaigns in Venezuela, Yemen, the Caribbean Sea and the eastern Pacific Ocean.

Hegseth said in a video on Thursday of impeaching: “Didn’t work against President Trump. Won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

Indivisible’s memo names impeaching Hegseth as a priority, as well as blocking a “business-as-usual” National Defense Authorization Act in the lame duck and refusing to fund the Department of Defense if “it doesn’t cut off money for the war.”

But it’s not clear that Democrats in Congress are ready to play that kind of hard ball. As they weigh their approach to the next era, they’re still half-stunned themselves by their larger than expected wins — and trying to put themselves in the best position ahead of the next elections in 2028.

GOP Rep. Christopher H. Smith of New Jersey told reporters on Thursday at the Capitol he hopes Democrats don’t hold up the NDAA “for the good of the country.”

“The NDAA is such an important bill for our national security, and it’s usually very bipartisan. I hope it is,” he said.

John Donnelly and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.

#6418. Hear stars being born in Chandra’s new sonifications

Every image of the cosmos is a translation of data. The X-rays collected by NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory and the infrared light gathered by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are invisible to our eyes, so astronomers assign them colors we can see. Even optical observations, from Hubble to backyard astrophotographers, translate, too, often assigning or enhancing color based on emission in various filters.

Sonification does the same for the ears, turning an object’s brightness, color, and position into pitch, volume, and tone. The idea dates back at least to the Geiger counter, invented in 1908, whose clicks intensify as radiation climbs. In 2020, the Chandra X-ray Center launched A Universe of Sound, NASA’s first ongoing program to sonify astronomical data.

Our ears are acutely sensitive to shifts in pitch, and researchers in fields ranging from astronomy to volcanology have found that listening to data can reveal patterns a visual plot might hide. Sonification also opens the cosmos to people who are blind or have low vision, for whom a processed image offers little.

RELATED: Listen to the universe: How sonification turns data into sound

On November 17, Chandra released four new sonifications, each built on a region where stars are forming right now. Young, massive stars blast out X-rays in fierce winds and outbursts, and studying those nurseries helps astronomers reconstruct how stars — the Sun included — got their start. Each piece pairs Chandra’s X-ray data with views from other NASA telescopes.

Each sonification plays as a short video. A line sweeps across the image, and whatever it crosses becomes sound. Most of the regions also come in three versions — Chandra’s X-rays alone, the companion telescope’s data alone, and the full composite. Try a single layer first, then the composite, and you’ll start to hear which sounds are associated with which kind of light.

At around 400 light-years away, the Rho Ophiuchi cloud complex is the closest star-forming region of the four. This crowded region is filled with a wide variety of stars. Chandra’s X-ray data identifies individual newborn stars, while JWST maps the other stars, gas, and dust around them. The X-rays ring out as bright, shimmering notes. Meanwhile, the clouds of dust and gas provide shifting ethereal chords, and individual stars land as crisp, percussive pings. Listen for the hush partway through — that’s a stretch of dark dust that hides almost all light.

About 1,310 light-years away and just below Orion’s Belt, the Orion Nebula is often visible to the naked eye and shows up in even the smallest telescope on a dark night. Chandra reveals more than 1,000 young stars here, each one sparkling in the sonification. Around them, the nebula’s diffuse X-ray glow holds steady as a ringing whistle. JWST’s infrared view of the dust and gas is audible as bent, warbling strings and a synthesized harp, reaching a crescendo in the nebula’s densest region before fading out.

Roughly 7,670 light-years away lies the ridge of gas and dust that became one of JWST’s most famous images when it was released in 2022. Chandra sees the scene differently, cutting through the dust to the hidden infant stars within it. Each of those stars plays as a quick stab, while the region’s faint X-ray glow draws out droning, unhurried notes — all played on an actual cello by musician Johnny Mok. JWST’s towering cliffs are a steady drone underneath, with new instruments chiming in briefly to denote a star or one of the cliffline’s jagged peaks.

Some 12 million light-years away in Ursa Major, M82 is the only object in the album beyond our galaxy. This starburst galaxy is building stars many times faster than the Milky Way. Its newborn giants burn out and explode quickly, venting superheated gas plumes that shine brightly in Chandra’s X-rays. Here, Chandra’s data joins Hubble’s visible-light view and infrared from JWST and the retired Spitzer Space Telescope. X-rays sit at the very top of the register, with the region’s busy center whooshing like moving air, filling most of the audible spectrum. It is punctuated by sharp, short stings from brighter newborn stars. The infrared rumbles below as a low hum interrupted by picked notes, and visible light fills the middle with a variety of sounds, including sweeping chords that rise and fall with optical brightness.

The Chandra sonifications come from a team led by visualization scientist Kimberly Arcand of the Chandra X-ray Center, working with astrophysicist Matt Russo and musician Andrew Santaguida of the SYSTEM Sounds project and consultant Christine Malec, a blind astronomer and musician. You can hear all four at the Chandra release page, and find the program’s full back catalog at chandra.si.edu/sound.

Where Chandra’s new album is composed by others, Skysynth lets you become the composer. Built by the same SYSTEM Sounds duo of Russo and Santaguida for the NSF–DOE Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s SkyViewer app, it lets you roam Rubin’s ultra-wide view of the southern sky — press Play to coast, or steer with your arrow keys or by dragging with the mouse. Galaxies crossing the center of the screen strum a harp and stars ring a glockenspiel, with color setting the pitch and brightness the volume.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

#6415. What satellites leave behind

It was the lithium that gave it away, says Daniel Murphy, an atmospheric chemist at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.

It was early 2023, in Fairbanks, Alaska, in the deep blue of winter, and Murphy and his colleagues had just sent a plane through the stratosphere, the atmospheric stratum 6 to 31 miles (10 to 50 kilometers) above Earth’s surface where the protective ozone layer lies.

Their experiment came as interest was growing in controversial proposals to cool the planet by injecting certain aerosols into the atmosphere — a form of geoengineering. The team hoped to get a baseline measurement of the chemistry of the upper atmosphere, before any geoengineering experiments altered the hard-to-reach atmospheric layer.

The team expected to find trace amounts of metals naturally deposited by meteoroids, which constantly bombard and burn up in Earth’s atmosphere. But their data showed way more lithium in stratospheric particles than is typically present in meteoroids.

“That’s what led us to the other metals,” Murphy says. Analyzing their samples, they also found higher than expected levels of aluminum, plus significant amounts of other metals like copper and lead that are scarcely found in meteoroids and must have come from some other source. Then there were the more exotic metals like niobium and hafnium, which appeared in their samples in the same ratio as in an alloy used to manufacture rocket engine nozzles.

The data pointed to an obvious culprit: human-made objects such as satellites and spent rocket stages that fall back to Earth from orbit and reenter the atmosphere. On the way down, they wear away and disintegrate under the heat of friction — a process known as ablation.

Later that year in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), Murphy and his colleagues reported that 10% of stratospheric aerosol particles carried metals from spacecraft.

The number was shocking, but not altogether surprising. Reentries have been rising sharply in recent years as corporations and countries began launching megaconstellations of thousands of satellites, like SpaceX’s Starlink. And all those satellites will inevitably deorbit.

Since Murphy and his colleagues’ 2023 report, it’s become clear that human-made satellites are now dumping more of certain metals into the upper atmosphere than meteoroids naturally do. This influx has raised concerns that the metals might catalyze chemical reactions that destroy ozone, alter cloud formation, or boost or buffer the greenhouse effect.

Researchers say it’s too soon to know for sure if the metals are a serious environmental problem. But megaconstellations are growing faster than our ability to close these knowledge gaps.

At the same time, the uncertainty over whether regulators might have to act presents a big risk to the space industry, says Martin Ross of the Aerospace Corporation, a research and development nonprofit based in El Segundo, California, and a co-author of the 2023 study. “We would call it an enterprise risk,” says Ross, “in that the longer we wait to see if there is something going on, the bigger the mitigation will be — if there needs to be any mitigation — down the line.”

From our vantage point on Earth, space may be incomprehensibly vast, but the orbital environment is not.

Six years ago, according to the U.S. Space Force’s public catalog, there were some 13,700 trackable objects circling in low Earth orbit; last year, the number had climbed to nearly 25,000. Disposing of satellites in the atmosphere reduces overcrowding and the risk of uncontrolled objects crashing into each other — and potentially setting off a chain of collisions that wipe out key space-based technologies or turn Earth orbit into an impenetrable debris field.

RELATED: Our increasingly cluttered skies

“Reentry is the only sustainable, short-term way of cleaning up the orbital environment,” says José Pedro Ferreira, a doctoral candidate in astronautical engineering at the University of Southern California (USC) in Los Angeles, who left an industry job for academia in the early 2020s when it became clear that reentry could have unintended consequences. “We need to do it, otherwise we may undermine our capability of accessing orbit.”

But operators are also typically held responsible by their national regulators for any damages their spacecraft cause on the ground, and for decades the industry has designed spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere to minimize the risk to lives and infrastructure on the ground, a principle known as design for demise.

As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

“As with everything, we live in a closed system,” says Ferreira, “and things do not disappear.”

SpaceX launched its first 60 satellites into orbit in May 2019 to bring internet to even remote regions of the globe; less than a decade later, Starlink’s constellation is more than 10,000 satellites strong. Starlink already comprises roughly two-thirds of active satellites, and SpaceX plans to grow it to as many as 42,000. Other countries and corporations are not far behind: Amazon Leo is authorized by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to operate roughly 7,700 satellites; China has plans to deploy some 28,000.

Not only are we launching more than ever, but we’re also bringing spacecraft back down faster than ever before.

For decades, spacecraft have been designed to burn up as much as possible upon reentry to minimize risks to those on the ground. As a result, the space industry has long perceived its impacts to Earth as minimal. But in the age of megaconstellations, that’s no longer the case.

Historically, satellite operators had what Ferreira calls a “gentleman’s agreement” to deorbit their spacecraft within 25 years of mission termination to prevent orbital clutter. Recently, some national authorities have begun enforcing even tighter timelines. The FCC, for example, now enforces a five-year window.

“If you have 50,000 satellites in orbit, which is almost surely going to be reached in the not too distant future, with a design lifetime of five years,” Murphy says, “that would mean a satellite would be reentering and burning up in the atmosphere on average more than once an hour.”

Operators of megaconstellations may use even shorter timelines for deorbiting satellites, according to Ferreira, bringing them down at the first sign of malfunction. “Which is great from a standpoint of orbital sustainability,” he says, “but it starts raising the question more and more about what the impacts are in the atmosphere.”

Aluminum, for example, which makes up the bulk of most spacecraft, may form aluminum oxides as it breaks down during ablation, which can kick-start a chain of chemical reactions that eat away at ozone, Earth’s main shield against UV radiation. Some atmospheric models suggest that metals from spacecraft in stratospheric particles could seed polar stratospheric clouds, further accelerating ozone depletion.

Injecting aluminum into the upper atmosphere is also the basis of many controversial geoengineering plans. Aluminum compounds would block radiation from the Sun, which could cool down our warming planet. But they might also entrap radiation reflected off the surface of the ocean, which could increase surface temperatures. Opposition to geoengineering has so far stymied any field experiments, but with the number of reentries rising from a few hundred to many thousands per year, an uncontrolled geoengineering experiment on a grand scale may have already begun.

“The metals are at the same altitude range as the ozone layer, so we have to be concerned about what they would do,” Murphy says. “We don’t know it’s bad, but we don’t know it isn’t bad either.”

One reason it’s so difficult to predict the impacts of ablation is that we don’t yet understand what happens to spacecraft during ablation. “We reenter things all the time and we have been since the moment we started launching spacecraft,” says Stijn Lemmens, a space debris mitigation analyst at the European Space Agency (ESA). “It’s fascinating, for something which is so ubiquitous, how little we actually know about it, and how little we used to care about it.”

Operators have long been incentivized to design spacecraft to burn up as much as possible in the atmosphere, and decades of this design for demise ethos has given the space industry a solid idea of how much material — or how little — will make it to the ground when objects burn through the atmosphere.

But in terms of that material that is ablated, “we’re really in the dark,” says Ross. Previous studies have suggested that around 90% of the bodies of orbiting satellites and spent upper stages could be vaporized, later condensing into the nanosized particles the team detected. But, says Ross, “we really don’t understand how these vehicles melt, how they break apart, how they form smoke trails.”

To quantify the impacts on the atmosphere, researchers start with atmospheric models and then add ablated material, examining how those particles interact with the natural stratospheric background via complex chemical reactions and physical processes like mixing. But the outputs of the atmospheric models are currently held back by our limited understanding of the fiery, complex process of ablation — details like what compounds are being emitted and what size particles are being formed. “We’re basically guessing at this point,” Ross says. “And we’re getting to the limit of what we can do with guessing.”

To do better, scientists are developing new models of the physics and chemistry of ablation itself. At USC, Ferreira and his colleagues model how ablation produces aluminum oxides in the upper atmosphere, providing atmospheric researchers with inputs for both emissions and particle size. In a 2024 study in Geophysical Research Letters, the team reported that a 550-pound (250 kilograms) satellite — about the size of your average megaconstellation satellite — could deposit some 66 pounds (30 kg) of aluminum oxide nanoparticles in the upper atmosphere. Such particles could remain aloft for upwards of 30 years, potentially catalyzing ozone-destroying reactions as they settle throughout the stratosphere for decades after reentry.

But state-of-the-art ablation models don’t always agree on what products are being formed, according to Ross. A model from researchers at the University of Leeds in the U.K. suggests that aluminum hydroxide, rather than aluminum oxide, may be the main byproduct.

To validate ablation models and get more useful data from atmospheric models, we need more measurements from reentries. How an object breaks apart as it tumbles through the air is a messy process — a product of astrophysics, fluid mechanics, materials science, and engineering. “You cannot reproduce it on Earth,” Lemmens says. “There is no facility large enough to, in one assessment, combine all the effects.”

That means scientists need to measure ablation where it’s actually taking place — “take instruments and put them on airplanes and go out and watch these things reenter,” Ross says.

Since the beginning of the Space Age, these kinds of measurements have only been taken a handful of times. Observing space objects from an airplane as they streak through the atmosphere is difficult work — and potentially dangerous. Most reentering objects are uncontrolled, making it hard to predict exactly where the object will hit the atmosphere and how much of it will burn up in the process. Researchers need a degree of certainty to avoid sending a plane full of scientists and sensors up into a debris field. “These types of reentries, which are destructive and still predictable so that you can get close, are extremely rare,” Lemmens says.

But in 2024, ESA got lucky. The first of four Cluster II satellites — launched in 2000 to study Earth’s magnetosphere — was poised to reenter the atmosphere, and the agency had a pretty good idea of exactly where and when it would break up over the southern Pacific Ocean.

“We could get close,” Lemmens says. “The drawback is it was in broad daylight, which had not been attempted before on this level of detail.”

In daytime, the team would have no visual confirmation of reentry, and it would be harder to get clean data than at night. The team had to trust they were pointing their instruments at the right spot, and then look at their data after the fact to see if they caught it. “In the end, it’s a leap of faith,” Lemmens says. “You predict as well as you can, you fly the plane as well as you can, but in the end, you do it all in the blind,” he says.

On Sept. 8, a team of scientists took off from Easter Island on a modified Dassault Falcon 900 business jet packed with instruments, and pointed their cameras just above the bright blue horizon roughly 500 miles (800 km) away.

The team used spectroscopic instruments to identify which vapors were coming from the ablating satellite. Since the team knew the material makeup of the satellite, they could gauge its surface temperatures during reentry, as the appearance of specific ions would indicate a certain material had reached its melting point.

Altogether, they captured about 20 seconds of the reentry. Two more satellites from the same cluster were set to reenter within 24 hours of each other on Aug. 31 and Sept. 1, 2026, giving ESA another opportunity to capture more of the reentry process and to fully reconstruct the breakup.

For researchers, one upside to the rapid and unmitigated increase in satellite reentries is more opportunities to capture the process in action.

Some of the best data yet to come will be collected by ESA’s Draco mission, in which the agency plans to build and launch a satellite with the “sole purpose of falling apart again,” says Lemmens. Draco will launch in 2027 with an indestructible capsule that will survive reentry, protecting the data collected from the surface of the satellite as it’s torn apart by the atmosphere.

Researchers will be able to combine these onboard data with remote observations, using them to improve or validate existing models of ablation. “That means we, for the first time, will actually have the full story without any ambiguities,” Lemmens says.

Once a scientific consensus is reached, then mitigation measures, whether technological or regulatory, can be deployed.

If research confirms that one material or another in spacecraft is particularly damaging to the atmosphere, for example, space operators can remove and replace it. “That was the basis of the success of the Montreal Protocol,” says Ross.

After scientists discovered a hole in the ozone layer in the 1980s, every country in the world signed on to the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement to control the ozone-depleting substances humans were emitting into the atmosphere. The hole has been shrinking ever since. Signed in 1987, the agreement is widely considered one of the most successful environmental treaties to date. Since then, however, other global climate agreements have not fared as well.

Still, many remain optimistic, including Ross. He points to the commercial space industry’s track record of working with regulators and astronomers to reduce space debris and light pollution. “There is some current flowing in those lines,” he says.

Some operators have already expressed a commitment to acting on whatever guidelines come out of research on the atmospheric risks. “The difficulty that I have as a responsible operator is, in this particular case, I don’t know what to do,” Vijay Thakur, a technical authority at French satellite corporation Eutelsat, said at an October 2025 panel at the Secure World Foundation’s 7th Summit for Space Sustainability in Paris. There are clear brightness limits he can follow to mitigate impacts to the astronomical community, he noted, but no such guidelines exist yet for atmospheric impacts.

“I want to put the right technical requirements, for me as the operator customer, onto industry so they can build what I need to operate and take it up and bring it back down without damaging anything from 0 kilometers to the von Kármán line,” Thakur said, referring to the commonly accepted boundary of outer space at 62 miles high (100 km). “Help.”

There are some design tweaks currently available that could reduce emissions and help more of each spacecraft survive reentry, including non-ablative heat shields and inflatable aerodynamic decelerators, according to Adam Mitchell, a materials and processes evaluation engineer at ESA.

Of course, the more of a spacecraft that survives reentry, the greater the risk on the ground during uncontrolled reentries — and most reentries are uncontrolled. “There is this balance between sustainability and safety, but when it comes to human safety, there is no compromise at all,” Chris Young, space sustainability senior lead at the U.K. Space Agency, said at the same Secure World Foundation panel. “Design for demise has to take priority.”

Satellite builders could also consider replacing problematic metals — but that comes with its own trade-offs. In 2024, the world’s first wooden satellite, LignoSat, launched to orbit in a partnership between Kyoto University and Japanese logging firm Sumitomo Forestry. A cube of magnolia wood panels, LignoSat will give researchers insights into how well wood holds up in the space environment, and how cleanly it burns up in the atmosphere. Carbon fiber is another material of interest, according to Ferreira. But these organic materials may release black carbon into the upper atmosphere, which may absorb sunlight or reflect it, depending on the structure the carbon takes.

Ross thinks we can close the remaining knowledge gaps in short order — and that those lessons can be applied almost immediately. “We can do that before the next generation of satellites comes along,” he says, “but we just need the resources.”

A cultural revolution is coming for the industry, regardless of what’s discovered about the impacts to the atmosphere. “The one-use, nonrecyclable culture that we have in space, of, ‘We’ll launch something to space with rare Earth minerals that are of limited supply and then burn them all up in the atmosphere after one use,’ that is unsustainable,” said Young.

A sustainable future — one that balances both Earth and space sustainability — will involve creating something we haven’t quite nailed yet in our earthbound industries. “We need to move beyond the single-use mindset that currently defines much of spacecraft design and accelerate the transition toward an in-space circular economy,” Mitchell says.

Can we do in space what we’ve failed to do on Earth? Right now, researchers are gathering data as fast as they can, as fast as resourcing allows, to inform models of ablation and atmospheric processes that will eventually be validated by measurements taken during reentry.

Then, equipped with actionable data, we can act.

Kate Wheeling is a freelance journalist based in Santa Barbara, California. She writes about the environment and humans’ relationship with the natural world. Her work has appeared in The Atlantic, Smithsonian magazine, The Daily Beast, and Mother Jones.

#6414. Meeks vows Iran votes as he seeks Foreign Affairs gavel

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., and staffers cheer as House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., takes the stage during a election night watch party in Washington on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Rep. Gregory W. Meeks, D-N.Y., the presumed next chairman of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, plans to bring resolutions to the floor to “immediately” end the war with Iran when Democrats take control of the House in January, he wrote in a letter Thursday seeking his colleagues’ support to become chairman.

The letter, which officially announced his bid for the chairmanship, lays out his oversight agenda for the committee, which will also see considerable turnover on the GOP side of the dais.

Meeks and other Democrats have repeatedly forced votes this year on war powers resolutions seeking to end the Iran war, with a Meeks-sponsored one clearing both chambers of Congress.

But those resolutions have been nonbinding concurrent resolutions, since the 1973 War Powers Resolution only lays out a fast-track procedure the minority party can wield for concurrent resolutions in the House.

With a House majority, though, Democrats could bring binding joint resolutions to the floor.

Beyond war powers votes, Meeks also promised public hearings on the war. He also vowed hearings on a range of topics including the administration’s Venezuela policy and “repeated defiance of Congress's constitutional authority over war powers and trade.”

“As chairman in the 120th Congress, oversight of this administration’s lawlessness and corruption will be at the top of the agenda,” Meeks wrote. “I will continue to advance a principled foreign policy grounded in our values, including support for Ukraine against Russian aggression.”

In addition to Iran measures, Meeks also promised legislation focused on “clawing back Congress’s proper role in the making of American foreign policy” and a State Department reauthorization bill that puts guardrails on the administration and protects career diplomats.

Meanwhile, the GOP side of the committee is poised to lose at least a dozen lawmakers — or about half of its members — next year between retirements and election losses.

The departures include longtime members such as former Chairman Michael McCaul, R-Texas, who opted not to seek reelection, and Rep. Scott Perry, R-Pa., the Freedom Caucus chair who lost his reelection race.

Several other Republican committee members remained locked in races that were still too close to call as of Thursday afternoon, according to The Associated Press, potentially gutting the GOP committee bench further. They include GOP Rep. Young Kim of California, the East Asia and Pacific Subcommittee chair who was trailing her in race against fellow California Republican Rep. Ken Calvert.

Rep. Christopher H. Smith, R-N.J., who chairs the Africa Subcommittee, lamented the turnover Thursday but predicted a lot of interest among remaining House Republicans to fill the void.

“There will be many who will want to be on it,” Smith told reporters. “We lost some really great people. Yesterday I can't tell you how sad I was about friends who are now not coming back.”

During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have discovered a mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo, an Anglo-Saxon cemetery in the U.K. that's famous for an enormous seventh-century ship burial of an early medieval king. The unusual grave does not have any bones but rather ghost-like shapes where a body was once buried.

Sand bodies were "burials where the bodies and bones had dissolved away in the acid soil, replaced by hard sand which held the form of the person, not unlike some of the bodies at Pompeii," Angus Wainwright, an archaeologist at the U.K.'s National Trust, said in a statement. These burials have been found at Sutton Hoo in the past, as well as at other Anglo-Saxon sites in the Suffolk area of the U.K.

The new sand burial, which was uncovered at a burial ground called Garden Field at the end of a 2025 dig, features in a four-part documentary created by the television series "Time Team" and archaeological experts with the National Trust and FAS Heritage. Whereas a 2024 excavation unearthed pieces of a bronze bucket used in a cremation ritual, the 2025 excavation was aimed at discovering evidence for the extent of the cemetery, when it was used and whether the people buried there were connected with the occupant of the famous ship burial.

"Until now, archaeologists have focused on the royal burial mounds," Wainwright said. In particular, experts have tried to work out who was buried in the "great ship burial" at Sutton Hoo. That person may have been King Rædwald, who ruled a kingdom in East Anglia and died around A.D. 627. The ship burial also contained an intricate and striking helmet. But the archaeologists are trying to learn more about the everyday East Anglians with the 2025 dig, which "moves the focus to these people and their ancestors and descendants," Wainwright said.

During the last week of the month-long excavation, the team unearthed the unusual sand body burial. Accompanying the deceased were grave goods, including beads, tweezers, a knife and a brooch, according to the statement. But directly underneath the sand body, the team found evidence that a second person may have been buried in the same grave.

"It was certainly a high point of this latest dig, to find another of these bodies in the Garden Field cemetery," Wainwright said. Experts think the sand bodies and cremations discovered in the burial ground may predate the famous ship burial.

In the first episode of a four-part Time Team series on Sutton Hoo, which launched on YouTube on Nov. 14, experts found new evidence that the people buried in the Garden Field cemetery were acquiring wealth and increasing their social status — so much so that they buried at least one person with a gold ingot.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The team also investigated the possible remains of a dock that was used to build and launch ships into the River Deben and found an unusual fragment of a cremation urn that surprised the archaeologists because it was decorated rather than plain.

"Well, it's at Sutton Hoo. Anything can happen," Justin Garner-Lahire, managing director at FAS Heritage, said in the video.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.
